title: Bi-Directional KV Transfers, Agent Trace Judges, and Prefix Cache Surgery
intro: Today's highlights focus on closing the latency and cost loops in agent architectures, from reversing KV cache flow in vLLM to auditing prompt-caching breakpoints. We also look at specialized evaluators for multi-step agent traces and a real-world multi-agent intrusion campaign.

stories.headline: vLLM adds bi-directional KV cache transfers to tame multi-turn TTFT
stories.summary: Standard prefill-decode disaggregation sends KV cache in only one direction, leaving prefill nodes to redundantly recompute prior responses and history as agent conversations grow. AWS contributed an accelerator-agnostic bi-directional KV transfer mechanism to vLLM via extensions to the NIXL connector and a KV-cache-aware proxy router. Under this flow, decode nodes retain KV blocks, stream back metadata, and let prefill nodes execute a remote read over RDMA before computing remaining suffixes. In benchmark tests on EC2 P5en instances using AWS EFA, this cut time-to-first-token by up to 1.6x on Qwen3-32B and up to 3.3x on GLM-5-FP8.
stories.why_it_matters: Multi-turn tool-use loops suffer heavy prefill latency penalties as context accumulates, making reverse KV reuse essential for responsive agent harnesses.
stories.reason: This directly addresses time-to-first-token latency bottlenecks in multi-turn agent harnesses by recycling KV cache states across turn boundaries in vLLM.

item.title: Improve TTFT for multi-turn agentic workloads with bi-directional KV transfer in vLLM
item.summary: Multi-turn agentic workloads reprocess growing conversation context each turn, driving up latency. See how bi-directional KV cache transfer lets prefill and decode nodes reuse previously computed context across turns, cutting time to first token by up to 1.6x for Qwen3-32B and 3.3x for GLM-5-FP8 on Amazon EC2 P5en instances with EFA.
item.content:
Multi-turn agentic workloads build on accumulated context as an agent reasons, invokes tools, and incorporates earlier results. With each new turn, the client resends the conversation history, including system instructions, prior prompts, tool results, and model responses, causing the growing context to be processed repeatedly. In Prefill-decode (P-D) disaggregation , each request is split across specialized nodes: the prefill node processes the prompt and builds its key-value (KV) cache, then the decode node retrieves those KV blocks and generates the response.

Conventional disaggregated serving, however, only transfers KV cache in one direction: from prefill to decode node. This one-directional flow creates two inefficiencies for multi-turn workloads. First, after generating a response, the decode node holds KV cache entries for both the prompt and the newly generated tokens. When processing the next turn, the prefill node cannot retrieve those entries, so it must recompute the KV projections for the previous response tokens. Second, the decode node maintains the session state while the prefill nodes don’t, increasing the probability of cache eviction for active sessions on the prefill nodes. On a full cache miss, the prefill node must recompute KV projections for the entire conversation history, including system instructions, prior user requests, tool results, and model-generated responses. As the conversation grows, this redundant work consumes more accelerator capacity and increases time to first token (TTFT).

When you build conversational assistants and agentic applications, longer interaction histories can increase latency and consume accelerator capacity through repeated prefill computation. In this post, we show how bi-directional KV cache transfer lets prefill and decode nodes reuse previously computed context across turns, which improves accelerator utilization and helps applications sustain responsive TTFT as conversations grow.

In our multi-turn benchmarks on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) P5en instances, bi-directional KV transfer reduced TTFT by up to 1.6x for Qwen3-32B and up to 3.3x for zai-org/GLM-5-FP8 (see the Performance data section). Results vary with workload and configuration. The instances are connected with AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter ( AWS EFA ), a low-latency remote direct memory access (RDMA) network used across servers in AWS. On supported instance types , AWS EFA supports GPUDirect RDMA and Neuron Direct RDMA to move KV blocks directly between GPU or AWS Trainium device memory on the prefill and decode nodes.

We originally built and validated the feature on AWS Trainium instance clusters connected with EFA and contributed it to vLLM as an accelerator-agnostic capability. The results presented here are from an Amazon EC2 P5en GPU cluster with EFA, showing that the benefits also carry over to GPUs. This post explains the bi-directional KV transfer architecture, router metadata flow, KV-block retention and recompute controls, performance results, and how to reproduce the benchmark.

Bi-directional KV transfer

Bi-directional KV transfer is a mechanism in which a decode node returns previously computed KV to a prefill node on subsequent turns of a conversation. This avoids recomputing shared context on the prefill node and is governed by a configurable KV recompute threshold. It mitigates both computational-redundancy scenarios described earlier. To make it work, the KV must survive past the turn that produced it and travel in the reverse direction, coordinated by a KV-cache-aware router.

NIXL KV connector enhancements for bi-directional transfer

We extended the NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) KV connector to let prefill nodes consume remote KV blocks, similar to how decode nodes already consume KV blocks that the prefill node provides. This is not a trivial change, because the two node types are architecturally different: prefill nodes compute KV representations for new prompt tokens and can provide complete prompt KV blocks. Decode nodes lack the capability (or efficiency) to generate complete KV representations and can only serve previously cached KV blocks. As a result, prefill and decode nodes still carry their own roles and logic for computing the metadata of remote and local KV blocks. The actual KV transfer mechanism (a NIXL READ), however, is common to both the P->D and D->P directions.

The following diagram first shows the existing flow in blue. The router sends the request to prefill node, prefill node computes the prompt KV and returns its block metadata, and the router forwards the request and metadata to decode node for the standard P→D NIXL READ. The numbered red path illustrates the bi-directional KV transfer additions: (1) decode node retains eligible KV blocks after generation, (2) returns their metadata in the streaming response, and (3) the router caches that metadata for the next prefill request. Prefill node then (4) checks the remotely reusable KV after it applies local cache matches, (5) queues an asynchronous receive when the reusable token count meets the threshold, and (6) performs a D→P NIXL READ before computing the remaining suffix.

Figure 1: Standard prefill-to-decode flow (blue) and the bi-directional KV transfer additions (red)

KV-cache-aware router

vLLM includes connector-side support for bi-directional KV transfer, while coordinating KV reuse across conversation turns requires a KV-cache-aware router. vLLM GitHub provides an example proxy that implements the flow used in this post which can be adapted for your environment.

The KV-cache-aware router is a lightweight, stateful control-plane component between the client, prefill, and decode nodes. It maintains an in-memory mapping from the client-provided conversation_id to decode’s kv_transfer_params . The router stores only block-location metadata, not KV tensors, and obtains that metadata from the response stream rather than separately querying decode node.

The following diagram shows how the router manages KV metadata across conversation turns. On the first turn, the cache lookup misses and the request follows the standard P→D flow. The router then saves decode’s metadata from the response stream. On later turns, the router retrieves that metadata using the conversation_id so prefill can reuse KV from decode. It then refreshes the metadata after generation for the next turn.

Figure 2: KV-cache-aware router metadata flow across conversation turns

Block retention TTL

Normally a decode instance frees a request’s blocks as soon as generation finishes. Under bi-directional KV transfer mode, it holds them for a configurable lifetime ( decoder_kv_blocks_ttl , default 480 seconds) and publishes their location and expiry. The conversation’s KV, both prompt prefix and generated response, then stays available for the next turn. For a turn that arrives before the time to live (TTL) expires, prefill node reuses the KV. One that arrives later falls back to normal prefill. Because this TTL is fixed and not renewed, tune it to the expected time between turns to balance KV reuse against accelerator-memory usage. A natural next improvement is to extend the heartbeat-renewed lease to the decode side. A decode instance could then reclaim blocks as soon as a conversation goes idle rather than at the end of a fixed timer.

KV recompute threshold

KV reuse isn’t always faster than local recomputation. For a short reusable prefix, interconnect and coordination overhead can exceed the time needed to recompute the tokens. The kv_recompute_threshold setting, which defaults to 64 tokens, controls this decision. Prefill node recomputes when the token count to compute is below the threshold and pulls KV from decode node when it is at or above the threshold. Deployments can tune this value based on model computation time, KV size, and interconnect performance.

related.title: Push-based KV transfer to improve TTFT and TPOT for disaggregated inference in vLLM
related.summary: vLLM's prefill-decode disaggregation splits LLM inference across engine instances but must transfer the KV cache between them. This post introduces a push-based NIXL connector that moves transfer coordination off the critical path, delivering up to 3x better TTFT and 30% better TPOT in benchmarks on Amazon EC2 P5en instances with AWS EFA.
related.content:
vLLM is an open-source inference and serving engine for large language models (LLMs). LLM inference has two distinct phases: prefill, which processes the input prompt and builds the key-value (KV) cache, and decode, which uses that cache to generate output one token at a time. These phases have different compute, memory, and scaling characteristics. Prefill-decode (P-D) disaggregation runs them on separate engine instances, allowing each phase to scale and be optimized independently. This can improve resource utilization, throughput, and latency under load. However, it also requires transferring the KV cache from the prefill instance to the decode instance before token generation can begin, making efficient KV transfer critical to time-to-first-token (TTFT).

One of the ways vLLM performs this transfer is through the NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) connector , which moves KV blocks over interconnects that support Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA), such as AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter ( AWS EFA , the low-latency RDMA network used across servers in AWS). On supported instance types , AWS EFA supports GPUDirect RDMA and Neuron Direct RDMA. NIXL can therefore transfer KV blocks directly between GPU or AWS Trainium device memory without staging through host memory. The default mode for NIXL connector is pull-based : After the prefill instance finishes computing the prompt KV cache, the router relays the source metadata, including the prefill block IDs, to the decode instance. The decode instance then allocates destination blocks, prepares the NIXL transfer, and initiates NIXL READ to pull the KV blocks from the prefill instance. Because these coordination and setup steps occur sequentially after prefill and before decoding can begin, they extend the TTFT critical path, as shown in the following timeline.

Figure 1: Pull-mode KV transfer timeline, where the router relay, decode-side allocation, and NIXL READ run serially on the path to the first token

This post introduces a push-based NIXL connector that moves post-prefill transfer coordination and setup off the critical path. If you run disaggregated prefill/decode inference with vLLM, push mode can improve application responsiveness by reducing TTFT and TPOT, particularly at high request rates.

In our benchmark on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) P5en instances connected with EFA, push mode delivered up to 3x better TTFT and up to 30 percent better time-per-output-token (TPOT) compared to pull mode (see the Performance data section) for the Qwen3-32B model. Results depend on workload and configuration.

We built and validated the feature on AWS Trainium instance clusters connected with EFA, and then we contributed it to vLLM as an accelerator-agnostic feature. The results here are from an Amazon EC2 P5en (GPU) cluster with EFA, showing the gains carry over to GPUs. This post explains the push-based architecture, transfer flow, threading model, performance results, and how to reproduce the benchmark.

Push-based KV transfer

This section explains the push-based design: its architecture, the transfer protocol, and the threading model that keeps KV transfer off the critical path.

Architecture overview

Push-based transfer improves TTFT and decode throughput for two reasons:

It removes the serialization of the pull model by overlapping producer and consumer work. The decode instance registers its target blocks in advance while the producer is still computing KV. The transfer then begins as soon as the producer’s blocks are ready, rather than after a consumer-side ID-discovery round trip, removing that round trip from the path to first token.

It moves the transfer-setup time off the decode instance. That setup runs on the prefill side and on a background thread. It prepares the NIXL descriptors and submits the transfer, so the decode instance does not spend those cycles during its latency-critical token-generation phase.

The net effect is lower TTFT and higher output-token throughput on the decode instance.

The push connector coordinates three actors: the decode instance registers its target blocks up front, the prefill instance matches each request and issues the transfer, and a dedicated background thread carries the KV write off the engine’s forward-pass loop. The following diagram shows how these pieces fit together.

Figure 2: Push-based KV transfer architecture, showing how the decode instance, prefill instance, and background transfer thread coordinate

Implementation details

The protocol has three logical steps.

1. Registration (decode side). When the decode instance allocates local blocks for a request requiring remote prefilling, it prepares a registration describing where the prefill instance should write the KV: its own identity and the block locations it has just reserved. Within the same engine step, the worker transmits this registration to the prefill instance as a NIXL notification. Because registration happens at allocation time, the connector knows the destination blocks before the prefill instance completes prefill.

2. Rendezvous (prefill side). The registration from the decoder and the completion of prefill on the producer can arrive in either order, and the connector handles both. If the registration arrives first, the producer holds it until its own prefill finishes. If prefill finishes first, the producer holds the request’s blocks until the registration arrives. Whichever event happens second triggers the transfer. The connector pairs requests by ID, and the matching accounts for reissued requests, correctly associating preempted or retried requests.

3. Transfer (prefill side). Once a request is matched, the producer establishes a connection to the decode instance (if one does not already exist) and issues an NIXL WRITE that copies the KV blocks directly into the decoder’s registered memory, addressing each destination tensor-parallel rank. The producer and consumer may use different internal block layouts. Each side maps block locations to its own physical layout at transfer time, allowing different block sizes on each side. Each WRITE carries a completion notification that NIXL delivers to the decode instance once the data arrives. The decoder counts these notifications, one per producer rank that writes into it. It treats the KV as received only after all expected notifications have arrived, at which point the request proceeds to decode.

Threading model

The push connector separates model execution from KV-transfer preparation by using a dedicated background transfer thread on each prefill worker. At the start of a request, the decode main loop allocates its destination KV blocks and registers them with the prefill instance while the prefill main loop computes the prompt KV cache. After both the destination registration and prompt KV are ready, the prefill main loop hands the KV blocks to the background thread and quickly returns to model execution.

The background thread establishes or reuses the NIXL connection, maps the request’s KV block IDs to memory descriptors, merges contiguous blocks into larger transfer regions, and submits the NIXL WRITE to the decode instance. When NIXL completes the transfer, it sends a completion notification to the decode instance, which then begins token generation. Keeping descriptor preparation and transfer submission off the latency-critical main loops prevents this per-request work from delaying model execution. The following diagram shows these main-loop and background-thread handoffs for a single request.

Figure 3: Main-loop and background-thread handoffs for a single request in the push-based threading model

Timing comparison of pull and push

stories.headline: Laminar releases flow-1, an RL-tuned model targeting agent execution traces
stories.summary: Observability startup Laminar released flow-1, an open-source small model post-trained with reinforcement learning specifically to diagnose step-level faults across multi-turn agent runs. The model operates within a harness called Signals, which treats spans like repository files and navigates compressed traces using targeted string search rather than brute-force context windows. Laminar claims the model matches GPT-6-sol in error detection quality at a 23x lower serving cost while outputting structured JSON signals. Traces with matching signal events are grouped into clusters to assist engineers in turning production failures into local eval regression datasets.
stories.why_it_matters: General-purpose LLM judges are often either too noisy or too expensive to run over every multi-step tool call in production traces.
stories.reason: It introduces a specialized RL-trained judge model specifically designed to diagnose and locate step-level errors in multi-turn agent execution traces.

item.title: Launch HN: Laminar (YC S24) – RL-trained model that finds errors in agent traces
item.content:
Hi HN, we’re Robert and Din from Laminar (
https://laminar.sh
). We’ve been building open-source observability for AI agents since 2024. Recently, we released flow-1, a model trained with RL to find errors in agent traces. On our benchmark (
https://laminar.sh/blog/flow-1
), it matches GPT-6-sol in detection quality while being 23x cheaper. This makes it affordable to analyze every production agent trace, without sampling.
Here’s a one-minute walkthrough: https://youtu.be/KJa3h6ZJNLQ
We also put together a post with example traces and analyses from flow-1 and other models: https://laminar.sh/blog/flow-1-in-action
Agent observability is crowded, so instead of a bullet list of how Laminar differs from X, we’ll explain how we’re solving agent observability from first principles.
Agents now run for many steps and fail implicitly. An agent can click the wrong button or cite the wrong document while every call completes successfully. These errors are the most useful ones to catch and understand. To find them, you need to understand what the agent was trying to do and inspect its LLM calls and tool results. Simply looking at the final agent output is not enough.
Collecting traces alone doesn’t solve this. A lot of agent observability platforms are still data collectors at their core. You can end up paying to store traces that nobody has time to read or extract value from.
Using another LLM to inspect traces is THE solution, but capable models are expensive at scale and cheaper ones often miss errors or flag unrelated things.
So we built our model to solve exactly this problem. We finetuned a small OSS model and then post trained it with RL on thousands of synthetic investigations of realistic agent workflows in software, legal, customer support, etc. We got a model that is both good at agent trace analysis and very cheap to run.
flow-1 runs inside a harness we call Signals. It acts as a coding agent, treating an agent trace like a repo, with each span (an LLM call, tool call, etc.) as a file. It starts from a compressed string representation of a full agent trace and a user prompt, then greps across spans and reads the relevant ones in full.
The beauty of Signals is that it can respond to a general prompt. You can ask it to identify user frustration, check whether your browser agent completed a checkout, and so on. It’s not limited to raw error detection. It returns findings as JSON in a schema users can freely define. We call these signal events.
Once you’re analyzing every trace, you also have too many individual events to read. That’s why we automatically group similar signal events into clusters. You can see recurring problems and how often they happen, then drill into individual events and the traces behind them.
You can use traces from a cluster to build an eval dataset for that type of failure. You can then use your favourite coding agent to hillclimb on those evals and check that the fix works across these cases before shipping it to prod.
Trace → analyze → catch errors and form clusters → fix → release. Making this loop easy is why we built Laminar.
We’ve put the same thought into the rest of Laminar. Our blog (https://laminar.sh/blog) explains how looking closely at how agents actually work led us to build 20x trace compression, a custom SQL query engine and automatic task extraction.
Laminar is Apache 2.0 and self-hostable (https://github.com/lmnr-ai/lmnr). We make money from the managed cloud.
We’d love to hear how you track your agents’ performance today. How much do you learn from user feedback versus your own monitoring? And when you fix something, how do you check that it hasn’t introduced a different failure?

stories.headline: Autonomous agent swarm breaches enterprise sites via exposed Cairn platform
stories.summary: AI security firm Norforge reported that a hacker compromised over 100 enterprise websites using autonomous agent networks orchestrated through exposed instances of Cairn, an open-source task-solving engine. According to reports confirmed by Cummins and covered by Reuters, targeted victims also included John Deere and SharkNinja, primarily hitting product support and third-party vendor sites. The campaign relied on fewer than 100 Chinese characters of operational instructions defining preferred intrusion tactics, with individual breaches taking roughly 23 hours of mostly autonomous execution. Norforge identified more than 20 exposed Cairn deployments with probable malicious intent, while Cairn's author reiterated that the project was designed as a general problem solver rather than an exploit framework.
stories.why_it_matters: This represents one of the clearest production demonstrations of autonomous multi-agent task engines being weaponized for long-horizon reconnaissance and exploitation with minimal human guidance.
stories.reason: A real-world security incident illustrating how autonomous multi-agent networks are now being deployed in production to execute coordinated, multi-target cyberattacks.

item.title: A hacker broke into John Deere and SharkNinja with an army of AI agents
item.summary: A hacker broke into more than 100 websites using an army of AI agents that mostly operated on their own, according to findings from the AI security firm Norforge. Though Norforge doesn't name the targets, Reuters reports that the victims included companies like John Deere, SharkNinja, and Cummins. Concerns over AI-powered cybersecurity breaches have grown […]
item.content:
A hacker broke into more than 100 websites using an army of AI agents that mostly operated on their own, according to findings from the AI security firm Norforge. Though Norforge doesn’t name the targets, Reuters reports that the victims included companies like John Deere, SharkNinja, and Cummins.
A hacker broke into John Deere and SharkNinja with an army of AI agents
The AI agents carried out the attacks with little involvement from the human hacker.
Concerns over AI-powered cybersecurity breaches have grown as the technology grows more advanced, with hackers using the tools to carry out large-scale attacks. At the same time, rogue AI agents are carrying out attacks of their own after escaping from testing environments.
Researchers at Norforge uncovered the attacks through exposed work on Cairn, an open-source AI platform that describes itself as a “general-purpose problem-solving engine.” With Cairn, users set a start and end point for the AI agents, which document their progress as they move forward with the task. However, as noted by Norforge, hackers can also use the tool to orchestrate cyberattacks using AI agents.
The hacker who broke into more than 100 sites was the “most active” among the exposed Cairn instances discovered by Norforge, waging attacks on companies based in the US, Canada, Australia, and Japan, as reported by Reuters. This attacker laid out “preferred intrusion tactics” using fewer than 100 Chinese characters, with successful breaches taking about 23 hours, according to Reuters. Overall, Norforge found more than 20 exposed Cairn instances that are “likely malicious.”
In a statement to The Verge, Cummins spokesperson Melinda Koski said the company “is investigating the report of a potential cyber-attack on a website operated by one of our third-party vendors.” A John Deere spokesperson told Reuters that there’s “no indication that sensitive information was accessed” as a result of the attack, while SharkNinja said the breach impacted a standalone site with product support information, and that it has contained the threat.
John Deere and SharkNinja didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.
Norforge says it’s working to get the malicious Cairn instances taken down. Cairn’s creator, who goes by @le1xia0, said earlier this month that the platform “was never a ‘hacking tool,’” adding that “misuse is a human decision, not a feature of the engine.”
Update, October 19th: Added a statement from Cummins.

stories.headline: Cloudflare cuts agent review spend 68% by repairing prompt cache breakpoints
stories.summary: Cloudflare published an optimization postmortem after costs for its automated code review agents doubled between April and August, climbing from $1.19 to $2.46 per review. While moving reviewers to Claude Opus 4.7 drove up raw rates, the core bottleneck was poor prompt caching in OpenCode v1, where session-opening system prompts had only a 14% to 26% cache hit rate. Because the harness combined static tool definitions with dynamic environment variables in a single system block with a trailing breakpoint, cross-repository prefix sharing broke entirely. By restructuring prompt prefixes, splitting cache breakpoints, and optimizing call frequency, Cloudflare dropped costs down to $0.77 per review while cutting median turnaround from 4m 09s to 1m 32s.
stories.why_it_matters: Even tiny structural flaws in how your agent harness serializes system prompts and tool schemas can silently nullify prefix caching and triple your provider bills.
stories.reason: A practical postmortem on cutting inference costs by 68% in production agents using prompt caching, cache-aware scheduling, and tiered model routing.

item.title: Cutting our inference bill by 68% by being obsessive about optimization
item.summary: When our AI code reviewer's cost per run doubled, we dug into the token usage to find out why. Learn how we used prompt caching and intelligent model routing to slash our inference bill by 68% while speeding up reviews.
item.content:
When we previously blogged about our AI code reviewer in April , an average review cost a palatable $1.19. By the end of August, that figure had shot up to about $2.46. We hadn't made any significant architectural changes: the coordinator was still handing work to the same set of specialist reviewers, and the same risk tiers decided how intensive of a review we gave.

Around mid-September we tasked our agents with working out where those tokens were going and cutting them — aggressively. With code quality at high effort, the average review now costs just $0.77, down 68% from the $2.43 it averaged over our two most expensive weeks before we started. Our main goal was to cut costs, but as part of this work we also managed to optimize the reviewer, so that the median review now takes just 1m 32s instead of the 4m 09s it took before.

About 40% of the savings came from changes and optimizations to the reviewer's code, and the rest from experimenting with which models we use and how much effort they put in.

How a review doubled in cost

The chart below shows the cost of an average review on each weekday since March. It holds the mix of review tiers fixed, so a day with more large reviews doesn't skew the data.

The cost per review steadily rose from $1.22 (March) → $1.44 (June) → $1.74 (July) and finally, to $2.32 (August). A small part of that is that more reviews landed in the most expensive tier (59% of reviews in March and then 65% in August). We believe there’s a simple answer for why: models are getting much better, and much more capable. Naturally, engineers are producing bigger, more complex changes which means more of them fall into our “full review” tier. We found that most of the cost increase actually came from model changes over those months, though.

At the start of August we moved every reviewer onto Anthropic models, which raised the cost per job from $1.38 to $2.03. We made this choice because we found that during our evals, Anthropic models performed better on this specific workload than other models.

Our internal standards reviewer, Codex , ended up on Claude Opus 4.7 due to a mix of performance and reliability. That took it from about $0.25 per review to $0.88 in August, which made it more expensive than the coordinator agent itself.

The cache hit rate also increased, going from 85.7% in April to 97% by September, while the number of tokens per review more than tripled, from 0.91 million to 2.99 million. A high hit rate on three times as many tokens still costs a lot more, even with the low cache read cost.

What else has changed since our last post?

One of the biggest changes is that the reviewer now runs on OpenCode  v2, which is a ground-up rewrite  from v1. Before switching all reviews over from v1 to v2, we ran every review in every canary repo on both v1 and v2 in a comparative shadow mode. The two agreed on the approval decision in 98% of the merge requests we tested, so we moved everyone over in one go in early October and removed the v1 code. Comparing two days with the same models, full-tier reviews on v2 finish about 13% faster. We’re also currently experimenting with other ways to run our internal AI reviewer, including solely on Durable Objects using pi-durable . We’re hopefully going to have more on this coming soon, so keep an eye out!

So, where were the tokens going?

Right before we started focusing on cost optimization, our AI review spend was split by: output tokens making up about 23%,  cache writes cost 43%, and cache reads cost 34%. This means that  most of the money was going on context the model had already seen or was about to see again.

That makes complete sense when you look into a single session. The code quality reviewer made 16.6 large language model (LLM) calls per review on average and over those calls it wrote 72k tokens to the cache and read back 1.08m, because each call sends the whole conversation as context. A session's cost grows with both the number of calls and the size of the context, and over the last few months we had slowly increased both.

It’s worth taking a few minutes to read about how Anthropic's prompt cache  works. It works by caching parts of the prompt that have already been computed by the large language model (LLM). These are known as prefixes, because they only work on the messages at the start of the conversation, not mid way through or the end. This means that a future request can reuse an earlier prefix, up to the part of the conversation that changes from what’s been cached. In our case, the harness tools, system prompt and messages at the start of our AI reviewer sessions rarely change, so they’re a great candidate for prefix caching. A prefix is only stored where a cache breakpoint ends it. Writing to the cache costs 1.25 times the normal input price and reading costs 0.1 times, and an entry expires after five minutes unless something reads it.

That means we had two things to work on: make the first request of each session read from the cache instead of writing to it, and make each session use fewer calls.

Sharing a cached prefix between every repository

Beginning September 14, the reviewer recorded the token usage of each reviewer's first LLM call, plus a hash of the first system block exactly as it was sent to the provider.

The data showed that the first request of a session found a cached prefix only 14% to 26% of the time. Every session starts with the same tool definitions and the same agent prompt, between 11k and 21k tokens that are identical in every repository we review, so almost all of them should have been cache hits.

The problem ended up being in how OpenCode v1 constructed the system prompt: It built one block containing our agent prompt, followed by an environment section with the working directory and the date, and placed the only cache breakpoint at the end of that block. The shared part was never stored on its own, so a review in one repository could never reuse what a reviewer ran in another repository had written.

On September 16, we added a marker to the end of every agent prompt and a plugin hook that split the block in two at that marker. The first half now ended on bytes that every job shares, and got its own breakpoint. To keep it that way we had to remove anything repository-specific from in front of it, so the list of available skills is disabled and tool descriptions can't change between jobs.

The same day we also moved our internal standards (Codex) reviewer's reference index (a table of internal standards, a skill file and a list of reference files) into its prompt. Until then every session had spent its first three turns reading those files with tool calls. Its LLM calls per run decreased from 15.9 to 9.6, and its cost per run dropped from $1.12 to $0.72.

Together these took the cost per review from $2.47 down to $2.02, and the drop was noticeable as soon as we kicked off the release.

Fewer calls, fewer dollars

The next set of changes went out on September 21 and 23. None of them were particularly impressive by themselves, but together they took about $0.20 off every review.

Change

What was happening

Effect of change

Removing tools that reviewers couldn't use

Sub-reviewers could see the tool that posts the final review comment. In 57% to 76% of sessions they tried to call it, were rejected by a check on the server, and spent another call recovering.

One wasted call gone, and about 2.9k fewer tokens of tool definitions in every sub-reviewer request

Reading files in parallel

In 64% of the code quality reviewer's turns, the model made exactly one tool call, usually to read a single file.

Reviewers read the shared context and all of their patches in their first response, up to 150 KB

Skipping reviewers on re-reviews

About two-thirds of our jobs are a second or later review of the same merge request, and often three of the reviewers have nothing new to look at.

On full-tier re-reviews, AGENTS.md reviews are skipped 56%…

stories.headline: LiveMACE evaluates persistent agent decision traces in non-stationary markets
stories.summary: A new benchmark paper introduces LiveMACEBench, an evaluation framework that pits persistent LLM agents against live cryptocurrency and US equity markets to diagnose execution capabilities over time. Rather than relying purely on outcome metrics like financial returns, the benchmark evaluates full decision trajectories across tool use, persistent memory, rule adherence, and multi-agent coordination. Over a 30-day live deployment across five frontier models, the researchers observed a marked divergence between realized profit and underlying mechanism competency. Traces revealed that identical market outcomes often stemmed from drastically different internal strategies, demonstrating that raw return leaderboards hide severe behavioral bottlenecks.
stories.why_it_matters: This provides rigorous empirical evidence that outcome-based agent evals fail to reflect genuine tool and memory competency in non-stationary environments.
stories.reason: A new agent evaluation benchmark that moves beyond outcome-based metrics to inspect step-by-step decision trajectories in non-stationary environments.

item.content:
LiveMACE: Process-Aware Evaluation of LLM Agent Capabilities in Evolving Markets
Abstract
LiveMACEBench evaluates persistent LLM agents in live financial markets using decision traces to reveal gaps between outcomes and underlying capabilities.
Evaluating agents by outcomes alone can obscure the capabilities that produce them. This problem is especially pronounced in evolving environments, where outcomes reflect a closed-loop interaction between agent behavior and changing external conditions. We introduce LiveMACEBench, a process-aware benchmark that uses live financial markets as a naturally evolving testbed for persistent LLM agents. Five frontier LLMs operate along continuous trajectories under matched Tool Use, Persistent Memory, Rule Following, and Multi-Agent Collaboration configurations. We evaluate them through both realized outcomes and mechanism-specific diagnostics derived from complete decision traces. Across 30 days of live evaluation, we find a pronounced outcome-capability gap: realized returns often diverge from capability-specific measurements, and similar outcomes can arise from markedly different patterns of mechanism use. Trace-level diagnostics further expose distinct bottlenecks across capabilities, demonstrating that mechanism access, effective mechanism use, and downstream performance are not interchangeable measures of agent capability. LiveMACEBench makes this distinction measurable, turning live markets from a performance leaderboard into a diagnostic environment for agent capability
Community
We introduce LiveMACE, a benchmark that uses live financial markets to evaluate LLM agent capabilities. Static benchmark questions can enter training data; future market events have yet to occur. This makes evolving markets a natural environment for testing how agents act under genuinely new conditions.
However, realized returns alone do not characterize an agent’s capabilities: they reflect both evolving market conditions and multiple aspects of agent behavior. LiveMACE combines simulated trading in cryptocurrency and US-equity markets with process-aware evaluation of four capabilities: tool use, persistent memory, rule following, and multi-agent collaboration. It records agents’ decisions and interactions, then evaluates the traces behind their outcomes.
Across five frontier LLMs and 30 days of live evaluation, we find an outcome–capability gap: higher returns do not consistently imply stronger capabilities, and similar returns can arise from different patterns of mechanism use. Our goal is to make live markets useful as an evaluation environment for agents, with measurements that go beyond the return leaderboard.
The framework is open source, and we welcome feedback on evaluating persistent agents in evolving environments.

stories.headline: OpenMobile-2 pairs Android environments with app-native tool APIs
stories.summary: OpenMobile-2 introduces an open mobile agent framework trained across MobileGym++, an environment featuring 35 simulated commercial apps alongside traditional Android emulators covering 110 total applications. Crucially, the system moves beyond pure vision-and-touch GUI loops by introducing hybrid execution, exposing over 300 app-native tool APIs across more than 50 apps so models can interleave direct function calls with UI taps. The release includes 12,000 fine-tuning trajectories and 2,000 verifiable RL tasks with automated reward signals. On standardized benchmarks, the model reached 79.9 on AndroidWorld and jumped from 31.9 to 59.6 on the real-device SPA-Bench suite.
stories.why_it_matters: Exposing structured tool endpoints directly alongside OS GUI actions is a far more efficient architectural paradigm for mobile agents than relying strictly on multimodal screenshot scraping.
stories.reason: Provides fully open environments and training recipes for training agents on app-native tool-use APIs rather than raw vision inputs.

item.content:
OpenMobile-2: Building Versatile Mobile Agents with Scalable Environments and App-Native Tools
Abstract
OpenMobile-2 is an open mobile agent trained with diverse simulated apps, large-scale supervised and reinforcement learning data, and hybrid GUI-tool use, achieving strong benchmark results and real-device transfer.
We introduce OpenMobile-2, a near-frontier mobile agent with fully open training environments and recipes. We make three key advances: (1) Diverse environments with simulated commercial apps: We build MobileGym++, featuring 35 realistic, functionally rich commercial-style apps with cross-app workflows, while preserving full controllability for reset and verification. Together with newly configured apps in Android emulators, this yields a diverse playground spanning over 110 apps. (2) Open training data at scale: Building on this foundation, we curate nearly 12K mobile interaction trajectories for supervised fine-tuning and the largest open collection of verifiable RL training data for mobile agents, comprising over 2K executable tasks with automatic rewards. (3) Hybrid GUI and app-native tool use: We explore an experimental mobile-use setting where apps expose selected functionalities as app-native tools alongside their GUIs, allowing agents to interleave GUI actions and tool calls within a task. We implement this setting in MobileGym++ with over 300 carefully scoped tools across 50+ apps. Additionally, we introduce MobileGym++ Bench for complex, long-horizon commercial mobile scenarios, supporting both GUI-only and hybrid GUI-tool evaluation on a shared task suite. OpenMobile-2 performs competitively across established benchmarks, including AndroidWorld (79.9) and MobileWorld (50.4), while showing promising transfer to real-device mobile use, nearly doubling SPA-Bench performance from 31.9 to 59.6. All resources are available at https://os-copilot.github.io/OpenMobile2-Home/.
Community
🚀 Introducing OpenMobile-2: Building Versatile Mobile Agents with Scalable Environments and App-Native Tools
We're excited to share OpenMobile-2, our latest work on mobile agents, with environments, data, benchmarks, and models fully open-sourced!
We explore two key directions in mobile agent research:
1. Scalable Training Environments. Existing emulator-based environments are heavyweight and cover limited apps, especially commercial ones. We introduce MobileGym++, featuring 35 high-fidelity, fully controllable commercial-style apps with cross-app workflow, built through human–coding agent collaboration. Together with emulator-based apps, we provide an open playground of 110+ diverse apps for scalable data synthesis and agentic RL. You can try our apps directly on the project website!
2. Hybrid GUI & CLI. While hybrid computer use is gaining traction, mobile agents remain largely limited to GUI interactions. We explore a new setting where mobile apps expose app-native tools, enabling agents to interleave GUI actions and tool calls within a task.
We also introduce MobileGym++ Bench, supporting both GUI-only and hybrid evaluation on challenging commercial-app tasks. OpenMobile-2 achieves competitive results on established benchmarks and nearly 2× performance on real-device mobile tasks.

stories.headline: TorchNeuron brings native PyTorch PrivateUse1 support to AWS Trainium
stories.summary: AWS announced TorchNeuron, an open-source PyTorch backend targeting Trainium2 and Trainium3 silicon that integrates via PyTorch's native `PrivateUse1` device registration. Developers can switch hardware execution paths directly using `.to('neuron')` or `torch.accelerator` without rewriting standard models or distributed code. The integration supports both eager execution (along with an experimental adaptive eager mode) and `torch.compile(backend='neuron')`, which lowers Dynamo graphs via Torch-MLIR to StableHLO and compiles NEFF binaries. Serving runtimes including vLLM Neuron rely directly on this compilation path, offering immediate support for FP16, BF16, and FP8 through TorchAO.
stories.why_it_matters: Native device registration reduces the integration friction for porting vLLM inference engines and custom agent serving stacks to Trainium without relying on bespoke vendor SDKs.
stories.reason: PyTorch's native Trainium integration gives inference engine builders a first-party path to run and serve PyTorch architectures on alternative silicon.

item.title: Introducing TorchNeuron: Native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium
item.summary:
Frontier models span language, video and audio, on architectures from dense and mixture-of-experts transformers to diffusion, state-space, world and structure-prediction models. PyTorch is where AI research happens, where the models...

The post Introducing TorchNeuron: Native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium appeared first on PyTorch .
item.content:
Frontier models span language, video and audio, on architectures from dense and mixture-of-experts transformers to diffusion, state-space, world and structure-prediction models. PyTorch is where AI research happens, where the models are defined, and increasingly where production happens too. Researchers want to experiment and innovate, and customers want the performance AWS Trainium offers to enable them to achieve their performance and scale goals. The training and serving libraries are written against PyTorch’s own APIs, and new libraries and new versions ship continuously. Over the last several years, PyTorch made those APIs accelerator-agnostic, with official extension points for registering custom hardware.

Today, to address the growing demand from the developers and research community on Trainium, we are excited to share an even simpler approach to program the chip as a standard PyTorch device, ahead of its open source launch at PyTorch Conference North America on Oct. 20. AWS Trainium is a portfolio of AI chips designed from the ground up for next generation cloud scale AI training and inference. We are announcing TorchNeuron , an open source native PyTorch backend for Trainium, so the model code, the libraries, and the tools you already use run on Trainium. This integration builds directly on the accelerator-agnostic extension points, including the PrivateUse1 device backend and torch.accelerator APIs, created by the PyTorch community.

TorchNeuron supports eager execution for research and debugging including new adaptive eager mode with improved performance, torch.compile for production performance, and the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) for custom kernels, on Trainium2 and Trainium3. Also, with Neuron Explorer , performance engineers use the same torch.profiler to trace execution from framework to hardware, linking every event back to its source line to pinpoint bottlenecks and optimize efficiently. TorchNeuron will be released as open source under Apache 2.0 at github.com/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx, going live as public Beta on Oct. 20.

“PyTorch’s vision is straightforward: developers should have a consistent experience across hardware platforms. Native support for AWS Trainium expands that choice, enabling researchers and engineers to experiment and iterate using the eager execution and distributed APIs they already know. Teams can take advantage of Trainium’s capabilities without reinventing their workflows or leaving the PyTorch ecosystem.” – Jana van Greunen, Director of PyTorch Engineering at Meta

Getting started: Easy device switching

Getting started is straightforward. Run your code on Trainium using the pointer: .to('neuron') .

# Run a training loop on Trainium
model = MyModel().to('neuron') # the only change
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters())
for batch in dataloader:
optimizer.zero_grad()
loss = criterion(model(batch), targets)
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()

Modern code written against torch.accelerator, PyTorch’s recommended device-agnostic API, runs unmodified. A compiled model needs the Neuron backend named, once with torch.compiler.set_default_backend("neuron") , after which torch.compile(model) takes it, or per call as torch.compile(model, backend="neuron") .

# Run a compiled training loop on Trainium
torch.compiler.set_default_backend("neuron") # call once, before any compile
model = MyModel().to('neuron')
model.compile() # no backend argument
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters())

for batch in dataloader:
optimizer.zero_grad()
loss = criterion(model(batch), targets)
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()

Capabilities

TorchNeuron registers Trainium through PrivateUse1, PyTorch’s official extension point for custom hardware, so the standard APIs work as written: torch.nn , torch.tensor , torch.autocast , torch.distributed , and torch.profiler all operate on the neuron device. The two execution modes of PyTorch, eager and torch.compile work natively.

High-level architecture diagram of TorchNeuron ( details ).

Eager

Eager runs operations immediately, so Python control flow, prints, and breakpoints all work with no compile or trace step. This is the mode for research and debugging. Eager mode dispatches operations individually. Executed directly, each operation compiles its own Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) file, launches it on device, and moves its intermediates through HBM. We are also introducing adaptive eager mode (experimental), to reduce the launch cost and provide better opportunities to fuse operations to approach performance of compiled graph without a code change, while retaining the interactive experience.

torch.compile

torch.compile(model, backend="neuron") captures the model into a graph the Neuron compiler optimizes, and is the mode for stable, high-performance models moving to production. torch.compile can be used to optimize the whole or part of the model and works seamlessly with eager mode. FlexAttention is supported natively. TorchDynamo captures the model into an FX graph, AOTAutograd traces the backward graph ahead of time, the Neuron backend lowers the result, by way of Torch-MLIR, into StableHLO, and the Neuron compiler produces a NEFF file that executes on hardware.

The Neuron inference stacks are built on the same torch.compile support in TorchNeuron. vLLM Neuron is a plugin to vLLM and serves LLMs; vLLM Omni Neuron is a plugin to vLLM Omni and serves diffusion models for image and video generation.

Ops and dtypes

Broad aten operator coverage for ops seen across text, multimodal and vision language, image and video generation and understanding, state space models, and world models. Models can use BF16, FP32, and FP16, with integer and boolean types, and torch.autocast and mixed precision code operate as written. TorchAO and FP8 are currently supported under private Beta and will be made generally available in the next release.

Distributed APIs

Distributed inference and training can use the standard PyTorch APIs and the high-level parallelism modules compose with your model as written: DDP, FSDP2, SimpleFSDP, tensor parallelism, and pipeline parallelism, along with common compositions like FSDP2 with tensor parallelism, ZeRO that are essential for training large models. DTensor and DeviceMesh are supported to handle sharding and the multi-dimensional process groups. The collective APIs (example: all_gather , reduce_scatter , all_reduce ) and the P2P APIs ( send , recv ) are supported. Collectives execute over Trainium’s dedicated collective cores intra-node and over the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) inter-node, so the communication transport is native to the hardware with no change to PyTorch APIs.

Streams and Events

Torch streams and events are supported natively. torch_neuronx.Stream and torch_neuronx.Event map PyTorch’s stream semantics onto Trainium’s hardware queues. Within a stream, data movement and computation stay in order automatically. Separate streams carry no implicit dependency on one another, so across streams you make that ordering explicit by recording an event on the producing stream and waiting for it on the consuming stream before using the result. The device-agnostic torch.Stream , torch.Event , and torch.accelerator entry points reach the same implementation, so code written against them runs unmodified. An error surfaces at the next synchronization point rather than at the operation that caused it; TorchNeuron tracks the earliest exception and re-raises it there with its original context. In execution, non-default streams multiplex onto a single hardware queue, so they keep ordering, priority, and event semantics but do not each get a dedicated engine; and when host collectives are disabled, a collective issued on a non-default stream keeps its place in that stream’s execution order but runs on the default hardware queue.

Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI)

The Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) lets researchers and developers develop…

item.title: “We were looking at it wrong”: The explosive claim that’s upended the AI world
item.summary: “I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at the AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the AI world on its head, sparking wild speculation as well as cautious (and not-so-cautious) celebration. Cammarata’s claim is…
item.content:
“I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at the AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the AI world on its head, sparking wild speculation as well as cautious (and not-so-cautious) celebration.

Cammarata’s claim is that LLMs might in fact be far easier to understand—and thus to monitor and control—than people previously thought. If true (and we’ll come back to that), it’s a huge deal.

After a summer filled with revelations that swarms of agents built by top firms like OpenAI and Anthropic have been breaking their containment and causing havoc on the public internet—often while those companies weren’t aware of what their agents were up to—the AI industry is desperate to get a better handle on the technology it has built.

That’s one reason the blog post landed with such force. “I think this may be remembered as a major moment in scientific history,” one AI researcher posted on X : “I feel like my understanding of what a neural net is has been catapulted into the future by five years or something.” Another called it “the most important AI paper of the year.”

Not everyone is convinced, however. What Cammarata has shared is little more than a hunch, says Chris Potts at Stanford University, who leads a team that is trying to understand how LLMs work. “As far as I can tell, nothing about this blog post makes the problems any easier,” he says. “It would not have occurred to me to say this at all, but very prominent people on social media seem to believe that it is an all-encompassing breakthrough.”

I talked to Cammarata the day after his post blew up. He says he was surprised by the response: “I didn’t expect people to update [their beliefs about AI] quite as much as they did.”

“I just really enjoy looking at neural networks,” he says. “Honestly, I really like doing this stuff. And after looking a lot, I have a hopeful story.”

Knotted networks

It has long been accepted that the mechanisms inside neural networks, the software that underpins most AI models, are very hard—perhaps impossible—to unpick fully. That’s because when the networks are trained, they appear to take on weird, tangled structures that make no sense to a human. Researchers like to say today’s AI is grown like a garden, not built like a bridge.

Cammarata has done more than most to establish that view. He previously worked at OpenAI, where he helped pioneer techniques that allowed researchers to peer inside models, including tools that can probe individual neurons to see what they represent. It’s a little like how neuroscientists use MRI to study brains. ( MIT Technology Review chose this approach, known as mechanistic interpretability, as one of its 10 hottest technologies of 2025 .)

Back in 2020, Cammarata and his colleagues were studying a small image-recognition model called Inception v1. When they looked at its neurons, it seemed to be using them to capture multiple things at once. For example, they found that one neuron responded to both images of cars and images of cats.

The researchers concluded that the model was getting at least some of its neurons to multitask, perhaps so that it could fit in more data. Looking at other models appeared to back this up. The phenomenon became known as superposition: Models folded unrelated concepts into single neurons. The upshot was clear: When you looked inside a model, what you saw was a vast, tangled knot.

Most mechanistic interpretability research has therefore focused on ways to untangle that knot . But despite a few breakthroughs , progress has been slow. Today’s models, such as the latest LLMs, are so large and complex that researchers can make sense of only tiny pieces at a time. Some leading figures in the field doubt if it will ever be possible to understand an LLM in fine-grained detail .

Cammarata was one of them. “I was very pessimistic,” he says. But then he took the trouble to really look.

Nothing but neurons

At Goodfire, Cammarata spends nearly all of his time peering inside neural networks. He has built new tools and deploys teams of AI agents to help him make sense of what he sees. “I spent like, I don’t know, 10 hours a day, seven days a week, for most of the last year just looking at neurons,” he says.

What he claims to have realized is that there is a kind of logic to neural networks after all, even if they seem to make no sense at first. “We were looking at it wrong,” he says. “I just think you want to try slightly harder; you don’t want to give up too quickly.”

Cammarata almost makes it sound like a conversion of faith. Those early experiments with models such as Inception v1, which suggested that neural networks were tangled up, fostered a kind of confirmation bias. When researchers looked at a new model, they expected to be flummoxed, he says. “Every time I couldn’t understand something, I was like, ‘Wow, this untangling process is even more important than I thought, because I can’t make any progress without it.’”

But the more Cammarata looked at neurons, he says, the more things started to fall into place. “Not all of them are flawless, but I expected nothing to be legible, or very little to be legible,” he says. “And actually, I was able to, like, map out whole circuitry.”

Back to cars and cats

Cammarata took his new approach—and his new agents—and went back to Inception v1. “I’d studied that for probably thousands of hours,” he says. But with fresh eyes, Cammarata found things that he now thinks they got wrong the first time around. Take the car-and-cat neuron. Rather than asking why multiple unrelated things were packed into a single neuron, he now tried to figure out what those things might have in common.

It hit him: It was a V shape. “I was looking at the same images; there was no technical change,” he says. “But I now believed that neural networks defined patterns, and so I looked at it differently. It probably took me five seconds.”

It turns out that the image-recognition model was packing cars and cats into the same place because pictures of both those things often feature a prominent shape that looks like a V: the face of a cat; the front of a car seen from the side.

Cammarata ran a few experiments to check what other things the neuron responded to and found they included the corner of a pool table, the pointed nose of a Japanese high-speed train, and a fire boat shooting water into the air from its deck. He also checked what turned the neuron off and found that it included images with a round O shape, a kind of anti-V.

The model had stored cats and cars in the same place because at some level they look the same, says Cammarata. “And I was like, ‘Whoa, okay, I think I might just be misunderstanding neural networks in general.’”

Cammarata is not saying that he yet fully gets how LLMs (or any models) work. He is saying that he no longer thinks full understanding is impossible. “I previously thought there would be some really hard problems to solve,” he says.

“I now feel like if I had 100,000 years to go look through a frontier language model just one circuit at a time, there’s, like, a pretty good shot I would come up with a good understanding.”

He adds: “And if that’s true, things are really good, because you’re about to get insanely smart agents at a ridiculous scale. And what would have taken me, you know, 100,000 years, we will be able to do much faster. Automated scientists are getting really good.”

Boundless optimism

Built by Google in 2014, Inception v1 is a far simpler model than anything at the cutting edge today. Cammarata and his colleagues have started looking at modern LLMs and plan to publish the technical results of that work soon. A lot of researchers are looking forward to seeing those details. “I appreciate that he looked at thousands of examples, but even a large number here is not a substitute for rigorous evaluation,” says Stanford University’s…

item.title: SciΠvot: Benchmarking Principal-Investigator Judgment at Pivotal Moments of Scientific AutoResearch Agents
item.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can keep scientific experiments running for months with little human supervision, but reliable autonomous research also requires scientific judgment. Evaluating scientific judgment is difficult because research decisions are open-ended and depend on project context. We construct SciΠvot, a 248-case benchmark of scientific judgment based on human corrections. The benchmark draws on records from six months of research in which senior researchers ran LLM agents on 26 projects across six scientific fields and repeatedly intervened to correct the agents' research judgments. In each case, an agent chooses between the original LLM plan and the human-corrected alternative, using only the project record available before the correction as context. We compare LLM and human performance and examine the effects of reasoning effort, access to the project record, and reconsideration. At medium reasoning effort with the project record, models systematically prefer the original LLM plan over the human-corrected alternative. Four of five frontier models perform below chance on the selected cases. The highest accuracy in the project condition across the tested models…

headlines.headline: PyTorch Adds Native TorchNeuron Backend for AWS Trainium
headlines.blurb: TorchNeuron provides a native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium, streamlining the execution of frontier architectures on the hardware.

item.title: Introducing TorchNeuron: Native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium
item.summary:
Frontier models span language, video and audio, on architectures from dense and mixture-of-experts transformers to diffusion, state-space, world and structure-prediction models. PyTorch is where AI research happens, where the models...

The post Introducing TorchNeuron: Native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium appeared first on PyTorch .
item.content:
Frontier models span language, video and audio, on architectures from dense and mixture-of-experts transformers to diffusion, state-space, world and structure-prediction models. PyTorch is where AI research happens, where the models are defined, and increasingly where production happens too. Researchers want to experiment and innovate, and customers want the performance AWS Trainium offers to enable them to achieve their performance and scale goals. The training and serving libraries are written against PyTorch’s own APIs, and new libraries and new versions ship continuously. Over the last several years, PyTorch made those APIs accelerator-agnostic, with official extension points for registering custom hardware.

Today, to address the growing demand from the developers and research community on Trainium, we are excited to share an even simpler approach to program the chip as a standard PyTorch device, ahead of its open source launch at PyTorch Conference North America on Oct. 20. AWS Trainium is a portfolio of AI chips designed from the ground up for next generation cloud scale AI training and inference. We are announcing TorchNeuron , an open source native PyTorch backend for Trainium, so the model code, the libraries, and the tools you already use run on Trainium. This integration builds directly on the accelerator-agnostic extension points, including the PrivateUse1 device backend and torch.accelerator APIs, created by the PyTorch community.

TorchNeuron supports eager execution for research and debugging including new adaptive eager mode with improved performance, torch.compile for production performance, and the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) for custom kernels, on Trainium2 and Trainium3. Also, with Neuron Explorer , performance engineers use the same torch.profiler to trace execution from framework to hardware, linking every event back to its source line to pinpoint bottlenecks and optimize efficiently. TorchNeuron will be released as open source under Apache 2.0 at github.com/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx, going live as public Beta on Oct. 20.

“PyTorch’s vision is straightforward: developers should have a consistent experience across hardware platforms. Native support for AWS Trainium expands that choice, enabling researchers and engineers to experiment and iterate using the eager execution and distributed APIs they already know. Teams can take advantage of Trainium’s capabilities without reinventing their workflows or leaving the PyTorch ecosystem.” – Jana van Greunen, Director of PyTorch Engineering at Meta

Getting started: Easy device switching

Getting started is straightforward. Run your code on Trainium using the pointer: .to('neuron') .

# Run a training loop on Trainium
model = MyModel().to('neuron') # the only change
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters())
for batch in dataloader:
optimizer.zero_grad()
loss = criterion(model(batch), targets)
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()

Modern code written against torch.accelerator, PyTorch’s recommended device-agnostic API, runs unmodified. A compiled model needs the Neuron backend named, once with torch.compiler.set_default_backend("neuron") , after which torch.compile(model) takes it, or per call as torch.compile(model, backend="neuron") .

# Run a compiled training loop on Trainium
torch.compiler.set_default_backend("neuron") # call once, before any compile
model = MyModel().to('neuron')
model.compile() # no backend argument
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters())

for batch in dataloader:
optimizer.zero_grad()
loss = criterion(model(batch), targets)
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()

Capabilities

TorchNeuron registers Trainium through PrivateUse1, PyTorch’s official extension point for custom hardware, so the standard APIs work as written: torch.nn , torch.tensor , torch.autocast , torch.distributed , and torch.profiler all operate on the neuron device. The two execution modes of PyTorch, eager and torch.compile work natively.

High-level architecture diagram of TorchNeuron ( details ).

Eager

Eager runs operations immediately, so Python control flow, prints, and breakpoints all work with no compile or trace step. This is the mode for research and debugging. Eager mode dispatches operations individually. Executed directly, each operation compiles its own Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) file, launches it on device, and moves its intermediates through HBM. We are also introducing adaptive eager mode (experimental), to reduce the launch cost and provide better opportunities to fuse operations to approach performance of compiled graph without a code change, while retaining the interactive experience.

torch.compile

torch.compile(model, backend="neuron") captures the model into a graph the Neuron compiler optimizes, and is the mode for stable, high-performance models moving to production. torch.compile can be used to optimize the whole or part of the model and works seamlessly with eager mode. FlexAttention is supported natively. TorchDynamo captures the model into an FX graph, AOTAutograd traces the backward graph ahead of time, the Neuron backend lowers the result, by way of Torch-MLIR, into StableHLO, and the Neuron compiler produces a NEFF file that executes on hardware.

The Neuron inference stacks are built on the same torch.compile support in TorchNeuron. vLLM Neuron is a plugin to vLLM and serves LLMs; vLLM Omni Neuron is a plugin to vLLM Omni and serves diffusion models for image and video generation.

Ops and dtypes

Broad aten operator coverage for ops seen across text, multimodal and vision language, image and video generation and understanding, state space models, and world models. Models can use BF16, FP32, and FP16, with integer and boolean types, and torch.autocast and mixed precision code operate as written. TorchAO and FP8 are currently supported under private Beta and will be made generally available in the next release.

Distributed APIs

Distributed inference and training can use the standard PyTorch APIs and the high-level parallelism modules compose with your model as written: DDP, FSDP2, SimpleFSDP, tensor parallelism, and pipeline parallelism, along with common compositions like FSDP2 with tensor parallelism, ZeRO that are essential for training large models. DTensor and DeviceMesh are supported to handle sharding and the multi-dimensional process groups. The collective APIs (example: all_gather , reduce_scatter , all_reduce ) and the P2P APIs ( send , recv ) are supported. Collectives execute over Trainium’s dedicated collective cores intra-node and over the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) inter-node, so the communication transport is native to the hardware with no change to PyTorch APIs.

Streams and Events

Torch streams and events are supported natively. torch_neuronx.Stream and torch_neuronx.Event map PyTorch’s stream semantics onto Trainium’s hardware queues. Within a stream, data movement and computation stay in order automatically. Separate streams carry no implicit dependency on one another, so across streams you make that ordering explicit by recording an event on the producing stream and waiting for it on the consuming stream before using the result. The device-agnostic torch.Stream , torch.Event , and torch.accelerator entry points reach the same implementation, so code written against them runs unmodified. An error surfaces at the next synchronization point rather than at the operation that caused it; TorchNeuron tracks the earliest exception and re-raises it there with its original context. In execution, non-default streams multiplex onto a single hardware queue, so they keep ordering, priority, and event semantics but do not each get a dedicated engine; and when host collectives are disabled, a collective issued on a non-default stream keeps its place in that stream’s execution order but runs on the default hardware queue.

Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI)

item.content:
A hacker broke into more than 100 websites using an army of AI agents that mostly operated on their own, according to findings from the AI security firm Norforge . Though Norforge doesn't name the targets, Reuters reports that the victims included companies like John Deere, SharkNinja, and Cummins.

Concerns over AI-powered cybersecurity breaches have grown as the technology grows more advanced, with hackers using the tools to carry out large-scale attacks. At the same time, rogue AI agents are carrying out attacks of their own after escaping from testing environments.
